To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a model of habitat connectivity based on a continuous habitat suitability model and gradient surface metrics is more effective at explaining gene flow in banded longhorn beetles than a patch mosaic model of habitat connectivity.

we compared the performance of a continuous habitat suitability model and a discrete land cover model in a landscape genetics study of the banded long-horn beetle, a species with high habitat specialization.

the continuous habitat suitability surface model (HSM), which was previously validated with genetic data, performed better than a discrete patch mosaic model (based on land use/land covers) at predicting landscape connectivity for the flower longhorn beetle Typocerus velutinus in Indiana, USA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of habitat fragmentation on species persistence.
the effects of habitat fragmentation on the population structure of the banded long-horn beetle, Typocerus v. vellutinus, in Indiana, U.S.A.
the question of how to model habitat connectivity and gene flow in complex landscapes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HSM-GSM model is the best performing model of landscape connectivity, followed by the PMM, the LCP model and finally the CD and IBD models.
the HSM-GSM approach is the best approach for landscape connectivity modeling for species with landscape complementation requirements.
the HSM model with GSM performed best at predicting the genetic distance between sites.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

landscape complementation is an important factor in landscape connectivity models and that the use of continuous habitat suitability models in combination with gradient surface metrics may be the most effective approach to model landscape connectivity in complex landscapes.
we have shown that landscape complementation is important for gene flow in banded longhorn beetles.
the HSM model is more appropriate than the PMM model to quantify the effects of landscape complementation on habitat connectivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the continuous habitat suitability surface, which we used to quantify landscape complementation, was the most effective at explaining genetic distances, followed by the patch mosaic model.

the continuous HSM surface with GSM might be a good choice for modeling landscape connectivity, especially when the landscape is highly heterogeneous and the species of interest relies on multiple, complementary habitats.

landscape complementation can be modeled using a continuous habitat suitability surface, but it is also possible to quantify landscape complementation using discrete landscape metrics based on a patch-mosaic model.
